title: “A Soul as Vast as the World”: Frantz Fanon and Humanistic Psychology (Editor’s Introduction to the Special Issue)
abstract: This special issue introduction by Leswin Laubscher and Derek Hook addresses the contemporary “Fanonian turn” in academic and clinical discourse, positioning Frantz Fanon’s work as a vital response to a global climate of systemic racism, state violence, and political silencing. Despite Fanon’s historical exclusion from mainstream Western psychology – a neglect the authors frame as a structural consequence of the very colonial dynamics Fanon analyzed – his insights into the “poetics of care” and the sociogeny of mental health remain profoundly apposite. The authors provide a biographical overview, detailing Fanon’s trajectory from colonial Martinique to the battlefields of WWII and his subsequent psychiatric residency at Saint-Alban under François Tosquelles. Central to the discussion is Fanon’s development of “sociotherapy” and institutional psychotherapy, which emphasizes that “curing the patient” necessitates “curing the hospital” and dismantling oppressive social structures. The abstract highlights the resurgence of Fanon in the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement, where his concepts of “combat breathing” and “new humanism” provide a theoretical framework for understanding the psychological impact of atmospheric violence. Ultimately, the issue seeks to integrate Fanon’s decolonial praxis into humanistic and existential psychology, advocating for a universalism premised on reciprocal human recognition and the ethical imperative of action.
